lessons.title: Water Requirements at Each Growth Stage
lessons.body:
Tomatoes need different amounts of water at each stage. From transplanting to first flowers, give about 1.5 to 2 liters per plant per day. This stage is critical for root development. In hot African conditions, water in the early morning or late evening to reduce evaporation. If leaves wilt in the afternoon, that's normal, but if they wilt in the morning, they need water.

During flowering and fruit set, increase to 2 to 3 liters per plant per day. Water stress now causes flower drop and small fruit. Keep soil evenly moist, not soggy. A simple test: squeeze a handful of soil; if it crumbles, it's too dry; if it drips, it's too wet.

When fruits are swelling and ripening, maintain 2.5 to 3.5 liters per plant per day. Irregular watering now leads to cracked fruits and blossom end rot. Reduce water slightly as fruits turn red to concentrate sugars, but don't let plants wilt.

In sandy soil, water more frequentlyâmaybe twice a dayâbecause water drains fast. In clay soil, water less often but deeply. A 20-liter bucket with a small hole can be a drip system for 10 plants. Always check soil moisture by digging 15 cm deep with a hoe. If the soil is dry at that depth, it's time to water. Remember, overwatering wastes water and causes root diseases. Underwatering reduces yield. Aim for consistently moist soil, like a wrung-out sponge.

lessons.title: Drip Irrigation System Design and Installation
lessons.body:
Drip irrigation saves water and reduces weeds. For a 10m x 10m plot (100 square meters), you need a main line, sub-main, and drip lines. Use 16mm drip tape with emitters spaced 30cm apart, each emitting 2 liters per hour. You'll need about 100 meters of drip tape for 10 rows spaced 1 meter apart, with 10 meters per row.

Start with a water source: a tank raised 1.5 meters above ground gives enough pressure. Connect a filter to prevent cloggingâa simple screen filter costs little. Then a main line (25mm PVC or lay-flat hose) to the plot. Attach a sub-main (16mm) and connect drip tapes using barbed connectors. End each tape with a figure-8 end cap.

For a 100 square meter plot, you need about 200 liters per day. With 2 L/h emitters every 30cm, each plant gets 2 liters per hour if you run the system for one hour. Run it twice a day for 30 minutes each in hot weather. Install a valve to control flow. Check emitters weekly: if flow is weak, clean the filter and flush the lines.

In Africa, many farmers use gravity-fed drip kits from local suppliers. A kit for 100 square meters costs around $50-$100. You can also make a DIY system using 20-liter buckets with micro-tubing. Place a bucket between two plants, run a tube to each plant, and adjust flow with a clip. This is cheap and effective for small plots. Always install a filter to avoid clogging from dirty water.

lessons.title: Monitoring Soil Moisture and Avoiding Overwatering
lessons.body:
Overwatering is as bad as underwatering. It washes away nutrients, causes root rot, and wastes water. To monitor moisture, use a simple soil moisture meter (costs about $10) or the feel method. Stick your finger or a stick 15 cm into the soil. If it feels dry, water. If it's moist, wait. For accuracy, use a trowel to dig a small hole and feel the soil at root depth.

Another method: a tensiometer, but it's expensive. A cheaper DIY: a wooden stick painted white, inserted 15 cm deep. Pull it out; if the bottom is dark and damp, soil is moist. If it's dry, water. Check every morning before 10 AM. In sandy soil, check twice a day.

Signs of overwatering: yellowing lower leaves, wilting despite wet soil, algae on soil surface, and fungus gnats. If you see these, stop watering for a day or two. Improve drainage by adding compost or raising beds. In clay soil, water less frequently but deeply. Never water at middayâup to 50% evaporates. Water early morning or late afternoon.

A simple schedule: in hot dry season, water every day. In cool season, every 2-3 days. But always check soil first. Keep a record: write down when you water and how much. After a week, you'll learn your soil's needs. Remember, tomato roots go 30-60 cm deep. Water deeply to encourage deep roots. Shallow watering leads to weak plants.

lessons.title: Mulching to Conserve Water
lessons.body:
Mulching is covering the soil around plants with organic or plastic material. It reduces evaporation by up to 70%, keeps soil cool, and suppresses weeds. In Africa, use dry grass, straw, banana leaves, or maize stover. Spread a layer 5-10 cm thick around plants, leaving a small gap around the stem to prevent rot. Organic mulch breaks down and adds nutrients. Reapply every 2-3 months.

Plastic mulch (black or silver) is also effective. Black plastic warms soil in cool areas; silver reflects aphids. Lay it before transplanting, cut holes for plants. It lasts 1-2 seasons but doesn't add nutrients. For small plots, use old sacks or cardboardâthey work too.

Mulching saves water: you may water every 2-3 days instead of daily. It also reduces weeds, so less competition for water. In dry climates, mulch is essential. Apply after transplanting when seedlings are established. Water well before mulching. Don't mulch with fresh green materialâit can rot and attract pests. Use dry material.

One caution: in very wet conditions, mulch can keep soil too moist and cause fungal diseases. If it's rainy, reduce mulch or remove it. In dry season, mulch heavily. Combine mulching with drip irrigation for best results. Mulch also prevents soil splashing on leaves, reducing disease. It's a low-cost, high-impact practice. A 100 square meter plot needs about 10-15 wheelbarrows of dry grass. Collect from around your farm or neighborhood.

lessons.title: Managing Irrigation in Dry Climates
lessons.body:
In dry climates like the Sahel, Kalahari, or northern Kenya, water is scarce. You must maximize every drop. First, choose drought-tolerant tomato varieties like 'Roma' or 'UC82B'. Plant early in the morning or evening to reduce shock. Use shade nets (30-50% shade) to reduce evaporation and heat stress. Shade nets can lower temperature by 5-10Â°C.

Water deeply and less frequently to encourage deep roots. In sandy soil, water daily but in small amounts; in clay, every 2-3 days. Use drip irrigation or buried clay pots (ollas). Ollas are porous clay pots buried to the neck, filled with water; water seeps slowly to roots. Each olla serves 4-6 plants. This saves up to 70% water.

Harvest rainwater: dig small basins around plants or use contour trenches. A 1m x 1m basin can hold 100 liters. Mulch heavily. Use windbreaks (trees or tall crops) to reduce wind evaporation. Water at night or early morning. Avoid overhead wateringâuse drip or furrow. If using furrows, water every other row.

Monitor plants for stress: leaves roll, turn dark green, or wilt. If you see this, water immediately. But don't overwaterâcheck soil first. In extreme heat, water twice a day: early morning and late evening. Keep a journal of water use. In dry climates, every liter counts. Consider deficit irrigation: reduce water during vegetative stage slightly to save for fruiting. But never during flowering. Test different schedules on small plots to see what works.

lessons.title: Water Quality and Testing for Salinity
lessons.body:
Water quality affects tomato growth. Salty water causes leaf burn, stunted growth, and small fruit. Test your water before using it. A simple electrical conductivity (EC) meter costs about $20. For tomatoes, water should have EC below 2.5 dS/m. If above, mix with fresh water or use salt-tolerant varieties. You can also send a sample to a local agricultural office for testing.

Salinity signs: white crust on soil, leaf edges brown and crispy, wilting despite wet soil. If you suspect salinity, test soil too. A soil test kit costs $15. In Africa, many boreholes have high salts. Rainwater is bestâEC near 0. If using river water, test during dry season when salts concentrate.

To manage salinity: leach soil with extra water every few months, but only if drainage is good. Add organic matter (compost, manure) to improve soil structure. Use raised beds. Mulch to reduce evaporation that brings salts to surface. Avoid fertilizing with high-salt fertilizers like potassium chloride; use potassium sulfate instead.

For small-scale farmers, a simple test: taste the water. If it tastes salty, it's likely too salty. But taste isn't precise. Better to use a meter. If you can't afford one, observe plants: if they show salt stress, switch to another water source or mix. Collect rainwater from roofs into tanks. A 1000-liter tank can supplement irrigation for a 100 square meter plot for a week. Always test new water sources before using on tomatoes.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Irrigation and Water Management for Tomato Farming in Africa

Water is the single most controllable input in tomato production â and in most of Africa, it is also the most expensive and most contested. A tomato crop needs roughly 400â600 mm of water per season, but how you deliver that water determines whether you harvest 15 tonnes/ha or 60 tonnes/ha. This practical reference gives you the numbers, schedules, and field-ready rules to irrigate profitably, whether you are on a 0.5-hectare plot in Kenya or a 10-hectare commercial block in Nigeria or South Africa.

Think of irrigation as a business decision, not just a farming task. Every cubic metre of water you pump costs money â fuel, electricity, labour, or pump wear. Every litre you waste through evaporation, runoff, or overwatering is a direct loss. Every day of moisture stress during flowering or fruit fill is a direct loss in marketable yield. The goal is simple: deliver the right amount, at the right time, to the root zone, with the least possible loss.

Water Requirements at Each Growth Stage

Tomato water demand follows a bell curve: low at establishment, rising through vegetative growth, peaking at flowering and fruit set, then easing during ripening. Your irrigation schedule must follow that curve. Applying the same daily volume all season wastes water early and starves the crop when it matters most.

Table 1: Indicative tomato irrigation schedule (drip, warm dry climate, medium soil)
Growth stage Days after transplant Crop coefficient (Kc) Daily water (mm) Interval Management note
Establishment 0â20 0.6 1â2 Daily (light) Keep root zone moist but not saturated; avoid collar rot.
Vegetative 21â45 0.8 3â4 Daily Deepen roots; avoid heavy pulses that leach nitrogen.
Flowering & fruit set 46â80 1.15 5â7 1â2Ã daily Peak demand. Stress here causes flower drop and blossom-end rot.
Fruit fill & ripening 81â120 0.9 4â6 Daily Reduce slightly near harvest to concentrate flavour and reduce cracking.

Source: FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 (Allen et al., 1998), Crop Water Information for Tomato. Values are indicative; adjust for local ETâ, soil type, and variety. fao.org/4/x0490e

Drip Irrigation System Design and Installation

Drip is the default choice for commercial tomato in Africa â it saves 30â50% of water versus furrow, reduces foliar disease, and allows precise fertigation. A basic system for 1 hectare includes: a water source and pump, a sand or screen filter, a mainline (50â63 mm PVC or layflat), sub-mains, and drip laterals (16 mm, 30 cm emitter spacing, 2â4 L/h emitters). Design for a flow rate that fills a block in 1â2 hours, and always install a filter â clogged emitters are the number one cause of drip failure on African farms.

Table 2: Typical drip system sizing for 1 ha of tomato
Component Specification Notes
Emitter flow rate 2â4 L/h Use 2 L/h on sandy soils, 4 L/h on heavy clay.
Emitter spacing 30 cm Matches tomato plant spacing on most beds.
Lateral spacing 1.0â1.5 m One lateral per row or per double row.
System flow 15â25 mÂ³/h Enough to irrigate in blocks of 1â2 hours.
Filtration 120â150 mesh screen or sand filter Essential; clean weekly.
Operating pressure 1.0â1.5 bar Use a pressure gauge at the filter.

Source: FAO Land and Water Division, Drip Irrigation technical guidance; Netafim and Rivulis design manuals. fao.org/land-water

Monitoring Soil Moisture and Avoiding Overwatering

Overwatering is more common than underwatering on irrigated tomato farms â and more damaging. Saturated soil suffocates roots, leaches nitrogen, and triggers fungal disease. The field test is simple: dig 15 cm down with a hand trowel. If soil holds together and glistens, stop irrigating. If it crumbles and feels dry, irrigate. For commercial blocks, use a tensiometer (irrigate at â30 to â40 kPa) or a capacitance probe. In sandy soils, check every day; in loam, every 2â3 days.

Mulching to Conserve Water

Mulch is the cheapest water-saving investment available to African tomato growers. A 5â10 cm layer of dry grass, maize stover, or straw reduces evaporation by 30â50%, suppresses weeds, and moderates soil temperature. Plastic mulch (silver-black) is standard in commercial production and can cut irrigation needs by 20â30% while reducing blossom-end rot and fruit cracking. Apply organic mulch after transplanting, keeping it 5 cm away from the stem to prevent collar rot.

Managing Irrigation in Dry Climates

In the Sahel, Horn of Africa, and semi-arid southern Africa, irrigation is not supplementary â it is the entire water supply. Key rules: irrigate early morning or late evening to cut evaporation; use drip or buried drip, never overhead; mulch every bed; and plan for a 20â30% higher peak demand in hot, windy conditions. Where water is scarce, deficit irrigation during ripening can save 15â20% of water with minimal yield loss, but never deficit-irrigate during flowering or fruit set.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Water Quality and Human Health

Never use untreated sewage, greywater, or surface water contaminated with human waste to irrigate tomatoes, especially near harvest. Tomato fruit is eaten fresh and can transmit Salmonella, E. coli, and cholera. Always test irrigation water for faecal coliforms before use, and stop irrigation with questionable water at least 2 weeks before harvest. Wear gloves when handling water from open canals or dams, and wash hands after field work. If you or your workers develop diarrhoea after handling irrigation water, seek medical care immediately.

Water Quality and Testing for Salinity

Salinity is a silent yield killer. Tomato is moderately salt-tolerant (threshold ECe â 2.5 dS/m, with yield declining about 10% per additional dS/m), but in many African irrigation schemes â the Nile Delta, the Senegal River valley, parts of the Rift Valley â salinity builds up season after season. Test your irrigation water at least once a year for electrical conductivity (EC), sodium adsorption ratio (SAR), and pH. If EC exceeds 2.5 dS/m, switch to salt-tolerant varieties, increase leaching fraction, and add organic matter. Never irrigate with water above 4 dS/m without a management plan.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • Know your stage: peak water demand is flowering to fruit fill (5â7 mm/day) â never stress the crop then.
  • Irrigate early or late: avoid midday irrigation to cut evaporation losses by up to 30%.
  • Check soil before watering: dig 15 cm; if it glistens, skip the cycle.
  • Mulch every bed: 5â10 cm organic or plastic mulch saves 20â50% of water.
  • Maintain your filter: clean drip filters weekly â clogged emitters cost more than the filter.
  • Test water annually: EC, SAR, and pH; act before salinity cuts yield.
  • Never use sewage water: test for faecal coliforms; stop questionable water 2 weeks pre-harvest.
  • Keep records: log daily irrigation volume, rainfall, and yield per block to find your true cost per kg.

Further Reading

  • FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 â Crop Evapotranspiration (free, official FAO guidelines and Kc values).
  • FAO Land and Water Division â Water Management (free technical resources on drip and irrigation design).
  • FAO â Deficit Irrigation Practices (free FAO water reports on managing limited water).
  • ICRISAT â Dryland Agriculture Research (free resources for semi-arid African farming).
  • CGIAR â Water, Land and Ecosystems (free research on irrigation and salinity in Africa).

Prepared for Rise Africa Skills â Tomato Farming Module: Irrigation and Water Management. All figures are indicative; always calibrate to your local climate, soil, and water source.

quiz.q: How much water does a tomato plant need per day during the flowering stage?
quiz.explanation: During flowering and fruit set, tomatoes need 2-3 liters per plant per day to prevent flower drop.

quiz.q: What is the best time to water tomatoes in hot African conditions?
options: B) Early morning or late evening
quiz.explanation: Watering early morning or late evening reduces evaporation loss.

quiz.q: What does it mean if tomato leaves wilt in the morning?
options: C) They have too much water
quiz.explanation: Wilting in the morning indicates the plant is water-stressed and needs irrigation.

quiz.q: How deep should you check soil moisture for tomatoes?
quiz.explanation: Checking at 15 cm depth gives a good indication of moisture at the root zone.

quiz.q: What is the recommended spacing for emitters on drip tape for tomatoes?
quiz.explanation: 30 cm spacing is standard for tomatoes, providing about 2 liters per hour per emitter.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a filter in a drip irrigation system?
quiz.explanation: A filter removes debris that can clog emitters.

quiz.q: How high should a water tank be raised for gravity-fed drip irrigation?
quiz.explanation: A height of 1.5 meters provides adequate pressure for drip systems.

quiz.q: What is a cheap DIY alternative to commercial drip irrigation?
quiz.explanation: Buckets with micro-tubing are a low-cost method for small plots.

quiz.q: What is a sign of overwatering tomatoes?
quiz.explanation: Yellowing lower leaves and wilting despite wet soil indicate overwatering.

quiz.q: How often should you check soil moisture in sandy soil?
quiz.explanation: Sandy soil drains quickly, so check moisture twice a day.

quiz.q: What is a simple tool to monitor soil moisture?
quiz.explanation: A soil moisture meter gives a quick reading of soil wetness.

quiz.q: What should you do if you see algae on the soil surface?
options: B) Stop watering for a day or two
quiz.explanation: Algae indicates overly wet soil; reduce watering to let it dry.

quiz.q: How thick should organic mulch be applied around tomatoes?
quiz.explanation: A 5-10 cm layer of mulch effectively conserves moisture.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of mulching?
quiz.explanation: Mulch suppresses weed growth and conserves water.

quiz.q: Which mulch material is best for adding nutrients to the soil?
quiz.explanation: Organic mulches like dry grass decompose and add nutrients.

quiz.q: What is a caution when using mulch in wet conditions?
options: A) It dries soil too fast
B) It can cause fungal diseases
quiz.explanation: In wet conditions, mulch can keep soil too moist and promote fungal growth.

quiz.q: How much can mulching reduce evaporation?
quiz.explanation: Mulch can reduce evaporation by up to 70%.

quiz.q: What is an olla?
options: A) A type of drip tape
B) A buried clay pot for irrigation
quiz.explanation: Ollas are porous clay pots buried in soil to provide slow irrigation.

quiz.q: In dry climates, what percentage shade net is recommended for tomatoes?
quiz.explanation: 30-50% shade nets reduce heat stress without blocking too much light.

quiz.q: What is deficit irrigation?
options: A) Watering less during vegetative stage
quiz.explanation: Deficit irrigation reduces water slightly during vegetative growth to save for fruiting.

quiz.q: What is a sign of salt stress in tomatoes?
quiz.explanation: Salt stress causes leaf burn and crispy edges.

quiz.q: What is the maximum recommended EC for irrigation water for tomatoes?
quiz.explanation: Tomatoes tolerate water with EC up to 2.5 dS/m; higher levels cause stress.

quiz.q: How can you test water for salinity without a meter?
quiz.explanation: Tasting water can give a rough indication of salinity, though a meter is more accurate.

quiz.q: What is a good practice to manage soil salinity?
options: B) Leach soil with extra water
quiz.explanation: Leaching with extra water (if drainage is good) helps flush salts below root zone.

quiz.q: Which fertilizer should be avoided if water is salty?
quiz.explanation: Potassium chloride adds more salt; use potassium sulfate instead.

quiz.q: How much water can a 1m x 1m basin hold?
quiz.explanation: A 1m x 1m basin with 10 cm depth holds about 100 liters.

quiz.q: What is the best water source for tomatoes in terms of salinity?
quiz.explanation: Rainwater has very low salinity (EC near 0).

quiz.q: How often should you flush drip lines?
quiz.explanation: Weekly flushing helps prevent clogging and maintains flow.

quiz.q: What is the recommended depth for burying an olla?
quiz.explanation: Ollas are buried to the neck so water can be added and it seeps out slowly.

quiz.q: What is the first step in designing a drip irrigation system?
options: B) Determine water source and pressure
quiz.explanation: Knowing water source and pressure is essential for design.
